title: The Great Stink: The Stench So Bad They Gave It A Name
summary: Guest producer Josh sits in with Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant to cover the Great Stink of London in 1858. They describe London's rapid population growth during the Industrial Revolution, the cesspool and rain-ditch waste systems, and the Thames becoming badly polluted and tidal. Michael Faraday's 1855 letter "Observations on the Filth of the Thames" and John Snow's cholera work tracing an outbreak to a contaminated public well are covered, along with the miasma theory. A summer 1858 heat wave made the stench unbearable near Parliament, which passed a bill within about eighteen days. Chief engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed an interceptor sewer system, pumping stations, embankments, and outfalls that still form the backbone of London's sewers. The episode notes the 1866 cholera outbreak in the East End, modern overflows, and the Tideway Tunnel "super sewer." It closes with a short-stuff plug about burning rivers and listener mail about the word "Yankee."

segments.title: Opening banter and London's growth
segments.summary: Guest producer Josh joins the hosts for banter, then they introduce London's growth from Roman times into a large city by the 1600s and its explosive population increase in the early 1800s during the Industrial Revolution.

segments.title: Cesspools, sewers, and the polluted Thames
segments.summary: Waste handling in London is described: Roman sewers, household cesspools that overflowed, and rain ditches draining to the Thames. The tidal Thames churned waste back and forth, and by the 1830s the river was dangerously polluted.

segments.title: Faraday's 1855 Thames investigation
segments.summary: Michael Faraday investigated the Thames in 1855 for the Royal Institution, using a white paper test, and published his observations in The Times about the filth of the river.
topics: Observations on the Filth of the Thames

segments.title: John Snow, cholera, and miasma theory
segments.summary: Cholera outbreaks killed tens of thousands of Londoners, and most people believed disease came from bad smells (miasma theory). John Snow suspected water and traced an outbreak to a public well contaminated by an old cesspool. Authorities had spent money on chloride of lime to mask the smell.

segments.title: The Great Stink of 1858
segments.summary: A dry spell and summer 1858 heat wave made the Thames stink terribly near Westminster, affecting Parliament. Politicians were forced to act, though the miasma belief meant people feared the smell itself as the cause of disease while poorer Londoners drank Thames water.

segments.title: Bazalgette's sewer plan and the bill
segments.summary: Parliament passed a bill within about eighteen days. Chief engineer Joseph Bazalgette, who had already drafted plans, was hired to raise funds and build a modern sewer that intercepted waste and diverted it downstream, away from the city.

segments.title: How the sewer system worked and its legacy
segments.summary: Details of the sewer system: gravity-fed tunnels, egg-shaped smaller sewers, pumping stations such as Crossness and Abbey Mills, Thames embankments, and outfalls. The 1866 cholera outbreak in the East End, which lacked sewer connection, supported the theory. Modern overflows and the Tideway Tunnel super sewer are discussed, plus a plug for a future short stuff episode on burning rivers.

segments.title: Listener mail: Yankee
segments.summary: A listener named Andrew comments on the hosts' use of the word Yankee and shares a regional joke; the hosts ask listeners for the joke's origin.
